| [LIT-714](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-714.md) v2 | The Method of Characteristics Revisited: A Viability Approach | Aubin (1999), lecture notes on arXiv. A set K is viable under a system if from each state in K at least one evolution stays in K, and invariant if every evolution does. By Nagumo's theorem K is viable exactly when the dynamics point into K's contingent cone at each state. The viability kernel of K is the largest viable subset of K; its complement in K is a repeller. The capture basin of a target is the set of states from which it can be reached in finite time. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-576](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-576.md)): the introduction and chapters 1–2 of the author's arXiv lecture notes, the parts that define viability. Worth reading as the shortest first-hand statement the record holds of Aubin's viability concepts: a set is viable if from every state at least one evolution stays in it, invariant if all do, and the viability kernel is the largest viable subset of a constraint set. Chapters 3 onward apply these to Hamilton–Jacobi equations and were not read. Stands in for the unread monograph [LIT-738](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-738.md). |

Unread: registered from metadata; the definitions are read in Aubin's 1999 mini-course notes [LIT-714](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-714.md). | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-05 from Crossref and the author's own list of his books, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. | [LIT-1292](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1292.md) v3 | A contraction based, singular perturbation approach to near-decomposability in complex systems | Bousquet & Slotine (arXiv 2015, unpublished). Recasts Simon's near-decomposability as a singularly perturbed system, fast module states x̃ and slow states y with ẏ = O(ε), and bounds the error of the reduced slow system with nonlinear contraction theory. If each module is contracting, the reduced slow system is contracting, and the coupling terms grow at most affinely in \|x̃\| and \|y\|, then below an explicit critical separation ε_c, after a transient of order (1/β_f + 1/(εβ_g)) log(1/ε), the fast states stay O(ε) from their quasi-steady values and the slow states O(ε) from the reduced trajectory, for all later time. A worked building example with a negative conductance shows multiple equilibria and instability above ε_c. Deterministic; bounds trajectory error, not dependence; proofs are sketches with a printed inversion in Remark 8. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1025](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1025.md)) in full; worth reading for the only rate the record holds for Simon's near-decomposability: with contracting fast modules (rate β_f) and a contracting reduced slow system (rate β_g), and coupling perturbations bounded affinely in the off-manifold state, Lemma 3 and Theorem 1 keep the fast variables within O(ε) of their quasi-steady manifold and the slow variables within O(ε) of the reduced system, uniformly in time after a transient of (1/β_f + 1/(εβ_g)) log(1/ε), for every ε below an explicit critical timescale separation ε_c = β_f / [χ_f(α_f,x + χ_g α_f,y α_g,x / β_g)]; and for Remark 6, that the micro states act on the macro level through their quasi-steady values, "an aggregation in time", not an ensemble aggregate. Read it knowing that it is a five-page preprint, never published in a journal, whose proofs are sketches; that Remark 8 prints ε_c inverted (the worked example's value √2/7 is the reciprocal of the printed expression, and matches Hypothesis 2); that Lemma 3's O(ε) bound on the slow error needs d_g = 0, which the proof's last line assumes silently while the worked example lists d_g = 1; that it is deterministic throughout and bounds trajectory error only, not any information-theoretic dependence; that the slow coordinates and the partition are given, not found; and that ε_c is sufficient and in linear checks conservative by factors of 3 to 50. |
| [LIT-1880](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1880.md) v2 | When Can Safe Controllers Adapt? Information before Commitment | Saligrama (2026). A safe adaptive controller must stay safe under every model not yet ruled out. Its first action that leaves no safe continuation under an alternative is a commitment, and the observation that action produces comes too late to justify it. With the information before commitment measured as a KL divergence between stopped records, every uniformly safe policy forfeits at least about ½e^{−I} of the value reachable only by committing. Acting on an exclusion at risk α needs about log(1/(2α)) nats beforehand. Bounded information and a linear gap give linear regret, shown for a headroom-limited device and for constrained linear regulation. Finite information can still certify a smaller candidate list. Safe recovery at O(√(T log T)) holds when a safe experiment is repeatable, informative and returns to a common state. | Active — read in full 2026-10-31 ([NOTE-1466](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1466.md)), with the main proofs; worth reading for the precise sense in which evidence must precede commitment: the observation a committing action produces cannot justify it, and bounded information before commitment leaves a fixed fraction of the oracle gap to every uniformly safe controller ([THEORY-1254](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1254.md)). It also proves the positive case, safe recovery from a repeatable informative experiment, and shows certainty equivalence failing at an active constraint ([THEORY-1256](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1256.md)). |
| [LIT-1893](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1893.md) v2 | Input-to-State Safety With Control Barrier Functions | Kolathaya & Ames (2019). Defines input-to-state safety for a safe set C = {h ≥ 0}: under an input disturbance bounded by ‖d‖∞, the larger set {h + γ(‖d‖∞) ≥ 0} stays forward invariant, for some class-K γ. A barrier inequality with a disturbance penalty, ḣ ≥ −α(h) − ι(‖d‖), implies it. Adding a damping term εL_g hᵀ to any barrier controller, or the matching constraint to a CLF–CBF quadratic program, gives ι = ‖d‖²/(4ε). The paper's examples show that nominal barrier controllers, including the standard quadratic program, can leave the safe set without bound under small disturbances. | Active — read in full 2026-10-31 ([NOTE-1477](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1477.md)); worth reading as the short statement of graded robust safety: under a bounded input disturbance a barrier-function controller keeps the state not in the safe set but in a set enlarged by a class-K function of the disturbance, and a damping term along the barrier's input direction delivers this with an enlargement of ‖d‖²/(4ε) ([THEORY-1267](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1267.md)). It is not the robust box invariance [CASE-190](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-190.md) certifies, which is [THEORY-134](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-134.md)'s. |
